fatal_errors: The central intervention is misidentified: the target uses an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy coating followed by a specific 550 °C anneal, whereas the hypothesis considers annealing bare commercial stainless steel.

The proposed governing cause—reduced grain-boundary elemental segregation—is not established by the cited evidence for the steels or treatments under study. E1 concerns selective dissolution of Cu-rich regions in compositionally different, as-cast high-entropy alloys.
The study omits the target's decisive hot-corrosion regime: cyclic exposure at 900 °C to Na2SO4/NaCl/V2O5 molten salts.

The experiment changes heat treatment and presumed segregation simultaneously, so improved corrosion behavior could arise from grain size, phase changes, residual-stress relief, sensitization, or oxide chemistry rather than homogenization.
explanation: The submission presents a scientifically plausible general hypothesis linking chemical homogeneity to chromium-rich passivation, and it proposes an untreated baseline, electrochemical measurements, and a nominal falsification criterion. It therefore has some value as an alternative study. However, it does not reconstruct the target system: it omits the AlCoCrFeNi coating, atmospheric plasma-spray parameters, 550 °C optimum, BCC/FCC structure, grain refinement, hardness response, and molten-salt hot-corrosion tests. Its high-temperature-water condition is not part of the target evidence. Mechanistic overlap is limited to chromium-rich passive-film formation; the target instead emphasizes coating-barrier effects, refined microstructure, Al/Cr-rich oxides, sluggish diffusion, and eventual salt penetration through pores and cracks. E1 provides only indirect support that segregated, acid-soluble Cu can harm corrosion resistance in other HEAs and does not validate annealing-induced homogenization or a self-healing chromium oxide on commercial steels. A more discriminating test would quantify segregation before and after treatment using grain-boundary-sensitive methods, include treatments producing similar grain size and phase constitution but different segregation, and test the actual coated and uncoated materials under the specified acid and molten-salt conditions.
